strengths: Gradient Slingshots offers a useful methodological contribution: shaping the optimization trajectory of feature visualization through weight fine-tuning without changing the architecture. This advances the practical threat model beyond conspicuous architectural fooling circuits.

The central attack is supported across CNNs and transformers. In Table 1, ResNet-50 target-image CLIP similarity increases from 0.53 to 0.69 while accuracy decreases from 76.13% to 75.13%. Experiments on ten additional output neurons and transfer to MACO strengthen the evidence beyond selected examples.

The accuracy–manipulation, model-size, and target-image studies provide useful information about success conditions and failure modes. Repeated visualization runs demonstrate consistency for the evaluated manipulated models.

The construction is clearly explained through equations and a toy example. Extensive implementation details, compute reporting, and a code link provide a reasonable route to reproduction. Limitations and dual-use risks are acknowledged, and no material ethical concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Preservation of internal mechanisms is not established by classification accuracy and class AUROC. These metrics can remain stable despite activation drift, added selectivity, or changed causal contributions. In the CLIP case, Table 11 sets w=1, eliminating the full-representation preservation term, while penguin AUROC increases from 0.50 to 0.62. Held-out activation comparisons and causal interventions would better support this central claim.

The theory-to-implementation connection needs clarification. Lemma 3.1 assumes an exact quadratic gradient field; the universal-approximation argument does not establish gradient approximation or compatibility at the piecewise boundary in Eq. (5). Moreover, Tables 11 and 14 specify a slingshot radius of 0.01 and per-coordinate initialization standard deviation of 0.01. Under the stated Euclidean-ball interpretation, typical high-dimensional initializations lie far outside that zone.

Arbitrary-image replacement is stronger than the demonstrated semantic redirection. Some high-resolution results reproduce textures or composition, and Table 21 shows no target-image CLIP or LPIPS improvement at the selected ViT setting despite improved text alignment. Evidence for internal-feature manipulation also rests on one constructed CLIP direction; the additional ten-feature experiment targets output neurons.

The proposed defense is a useful cross-check but lacks a quantitative detection evaluation. Pre/post top-k overlap measures ranking stability, without establishing detection rates or false-positive rates when an auditor receives only the manipulated model. Clean-model disagreement controls and an operational detection rule are missing. The SAE/LRP auditing pipeline described in Section 5 is also hypothetical, making the claim that discovery becomes 'effectively impossible' insufficiently supported.

The ProxPulse comparison covers one neuron–target pair and two baseline settings, whereas GS receives extensive tuning. Matched tuning budgets and ablations separating the tunnel construction from the preservation objective would clarify the source of improvement. Reported variability primarily concerns repeated FV generation, leaving robustness across independent attack-training runs uncertain.

Several reporting inconsistencies affect reproducibility: Table 3 states 100 independent runs, whereas Section C.8 specifies 30 CLIP runs; Section 5 uses 0.1% of ImageNet for preservation, whereas Table 10 specifies 0.28%. These should be reconciled with the actual experiments.
